rationale.conceptual: The method uses standard techniques from condensed matter physics (free-fermion diagonalization, BCS gap equation) with a minor custom twist (the spin-flip energy bound). A graduate student familiar with many-body numerical methods would find this straightforward to implement.
rationale.execution: The pipeline has 4 distinct but simple steps (energy bound, critical filling extraction, BCS self-consistency, symmetry report) that can be done in a single Python script. Only numpy/scipy are needed; no complex data handling, orchestration, or environment dependencies.

difficulty.reasoning: The task involves implementing a free-fermion tight-binding model diagonalization and BCS mean-field self-consistency equations. Both are standard techniques in condensed matter theory; the conceptual novelty lies in the custom energy bound, but the computational steps are routine. Execution is a simple 4-step pipeline with standard libraries, outputting CSV/JSON/TXT files. Resource needs are moderate: sparse matrix diagonalization on up to 40k dimensions and low-dimensional BCS integrals, all CPU-bound.

compute_estimate.reasoning: The largest computation is the free-fermion ground-state diagonalization on a lattice of up to ~40,000 sites, requiring a sparse Hermitian eigensolver on a single CPU. The BCS self-consistency involves 2D momentum integrals on modest grids. Peak memory is a few GB, no GPU needed.
